groups.name: Foundations
groups.blurb: Start here! The building blocks every mathematician needs.

groups.name: Algebra
groups.blurb: Letters that stand for numbers, and the puzzles they solve.

groups.name: Geometry
groups.blurb: Shapes, maps, curved worlds and never-ending patterns.

groups.name: Advanced
groups.blurb: Ready for a challenge? Big ideas from real mathematicians.

topics.name: Arithmetic
topics.blurb: Undo operations, master exponents and negative numbers, and solve your first equations!

pics.alt: A wooden abacus with beads being used on a shop counter
pics.caption: A real abacus at a kimono shop in Otaru, Japan. Shopkeepers there have used the soroban abacus for hundreds of years, sliding beads to add and subtract super fast!

pics.alt: An old brown bone with rows of scratched tally marks
pics.caption: The Ishango bone, found in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It's about 20,000 years old, and its scratched tally marks may be one of the oldest records of counting!

topics.name: Fractions
topics.blurb: Fractions are just division in disguise. Add, multiply, divide and solve with them!

pics.alt: A round pizza split into four parts, each with different toppings
pics.caption: A "four seasons" pizza has 4 parts with different toppings, so each part is about 1/4 of the pizza. Two parts together make 2/4, which is the same as 1/2!

pics.alt: Eleven circles, each cut into equal slices with one slice shaded green
pics.caption: Fraction circles from 1/2 all the way to 1/12. Notice that the more slices you cut, the smaller each slice gets!

topics.name: Logic
topics.blurb: AND, OR, NOT and IF-THEN: think like a detective and solve knights-and-knaves puzzles!

pics.alt: A marble bust of a bearded man from ancient Greece
pics.caption: A marble bust of Aristotle (384–322 BC), the ancient Greek thinker who wrote down some of the very first rules of logic.

pics.alt: A hand-coloured engraving of a man in a dark jacket and bow tie
pics.caption: George Boole (1815–1864) turned logic into algebra with just TRUE and FALSE. Every computer today runs on his "Boolean logic"!

topics.name: Algebraic Equations
topics.blurb: Keep the balance! Crack equations with fractions, negatives, x on both sides and more.

pics.alt: A metal balance scale with two pans
pics.caption: A balance scale stays level only when both sides weigh the same, just like the two sides of an equation. That's the Golden Rule of algebra!

pics.alt: A printed page of Arabic text
pics.caption: A printed page from an 1831 edition of al-Khwarizmi's famous book about solving equations, which he wrote in Baghdad around 820 AD. The word "algebra" comes from "al-jabr" in its title!

topics.name: Linear Functions
topics.blurb: Function machines, slope and straight-line graphs, from f(x) to systems of equations.

pics.alt: A grid graph with a red line and a blue line crossing
pics.caption: Two linear functions, y = ½x + 2 and y = −x + 5. Every linear function draws a perfectly straight line, and these two meet at the point (2, 3)!

pics.alt: A diagram of a tilted line with its rise and run marked
pics.caption: Slope is rise ÷ run: how far a line goes up (Δy) for each step it goes across (Δx).

topics.name: Logarithms
topics.blurb: The backwards question: what power do I need? Logs turn multiplying into adding!

pics.alt: Portrait of John Napier, a bearded man with a ruff collar
pics.caption: John Napier (1550–1617) of Scotland invented logarithms and published them in 1614 to make huge multiplications much easier.

pics.alt: A long slide rule covered in number scales
pics.caption: A slide rule. Before calculators, scientists and engineers multiplied numbers by sliding logarithm scales against each other!

topics.name: Exponential Growth
topics.blurb: Doubling machines! See how numbers explode (and shrink) with f(x) = a × bˣ.

pics.alt: A wooden chessboard with 1, 2, 4 and 8 grains of rice on the first squares
pics.caption: The wheat and chessboard puzzle: put 1 grain on the first square, 2 on the next, then 4, 8, 16... By the last square you'd need more than 18 quintillion grains in total!

pics.alt: Rod-shaped bacteria seen up close through a microscope
pics.caption: E. coli bacteria seen through a microscope. With plenty of food, each one can split in two about every 20 minutes. That's exponential growth!

topics.name: Pascal's Triangle
topics.blurb: A simple triangle of numbers that hides counting secrets, powers of 2 and the hockey stick!

pics.alt: Portrait of Blaise Pascal, a man with long hair
pics.caption: Blaise Pascal (1623–1662), the French mathematician the triangle is named after. As a teenager he also built one of the first mechanical calculators!

pics.alt: An old Chinese drawing of a triangle of numbers made of circles
pics.caption: The same triangle in a Chinese book from 1303. Chinese mathematicians like Yang Hui knew about it hundreds of years before Pascal was born!

topics.name: Geometry
topics.blurb: Angles, triangles, Pythagoras, circles and more, with real proofs you can follow.

pics.alt: A small, torn piece of ancient papyrus with Greek writing and a diagram
pics.caption: A scrap of papyrus from Oxyrhynchus, Egypt, written around 100 AD. It has a diagram from Euclid's Elements and is one of the oldest pieces of Euclid ever found!

pics.alt: The great pyramids of Giza in the desert
pics.caption: The pyramids of Giza in Egypt, built about 4,500 years ago. Their builders needed geometry to make the sides and corners so precise!

topics.name: Algebraic Geometry
topics.blurb: Give every point an address (x, y) and watch equations draw lines, circles and parabolas!

pics.alt: Portrait of René Descartes, a man with long dark hair and a moustache
pics.caption: René Descartes (1596–1650) had the idea of giving every point an address (x, y). That's why it's called the Cartesian plane!

pics.alt: A coordinate plane with x and y axes and four coloured points
pics.caption: The coordinate plane: two number lines that cross at zero. Every point has its own (x, y) address, like (2, 3) or (−3, 1)!

topics.name: Non-Euclidean Geometry
topics.blurb: What if space is curved? Triangles on balls and saddles break the 180° rule!

pics.alt: A globe with a giant triangle drawn on it, with angles of 90, 90 and 50 degrees
pics.caption: A giant triangle drawn on the Earth. Its angles are 90° + 90° + 50° = 230°, way more than 180°! But a small triangle on the ground is almost flat, so its angles add up to about 180°.

pics.alt: A circle filled with colourful triangle tiles that get tinier near the edge
pics.caption: A tiling of the hyperbolic plane. The tiles near the edge look tiny to us, but in their own curved world they're all exactly the same size!

topics.name: Fractal Geometry
topics.blurb: Shapes made of smaller copies of themselves, from snowflakes to broccoli!

pics.alt: A bright green Romanesco broccoli with spiky spiral bumps
pics.caption: Romanesco broccoli: each bump is made of smaller bumps that look like the whole thing. It's a fractal you can eat!

pics.alt: A black shape with swirling coloured edges
pics.caption: The Mandelbrot set, the most famous fractal of all. You can zoom into its edge forever and keep finding new swirls!

topics.name: Calculus
topics.blurb: The math of change: limits, derivatives, areas and the Fundamental Theorem.

pics.alt: Portrait of Isaac Newton, a man with long grey hair
pics.caption: Isaac Newton (1643–1727), painted in 1689. He invented calculus to explain how planets and falling apples move.

pics.alt: Portrait of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in a huge curly wig
pics.caption: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) invented calculus too, at about the same time. We still use his dy/dx and ∫ symbols today!

topics.name: Complex Analysis
topics.blurb: Meet i, the number whose square is −1, and see how multiplying can spin and stretch!

pics.alt: Portrait of Leonhard Euler wearing a cloth cap
pics.caption: Leonhard Euler (1707–1783), one of the greatest mathematicians ever. He was the first to use the letter i for √−1!

pics.alt: A square picture full of rainbow colours swirling around several points
pics.caption: A picture of a complex function. Each colour shows the direction of a complex number, so the rainbow swirls show where the function spins around!

topics.name: Matrix Math
topics.blurb: Grids of numbers that power video games, photos and secret codes!

pics.alt: A diagram showing a row of one matrix meeting a column of another
pics.caption: How matrix multiplication works: each row of matrix A meets a column of matrix B to make one square in the answer.

pics.alt: A drawing of a computer, with a zoomed-in square showing tiny coloured blocks
pics.caption: Zoom in on any computer picture and you'll see it's really a grid of tiny squares called pixels: a giant matrix of numbers!

topics.name: Number Theory
topics.blurb: Primes, divisibility rules, GCF, LCM and Euclid's amazing 2,300-year-old algorithm.

pics.alt: An animated grid of numbers where multiples get crossed out and the primes stay
pics.caption: The Sieve of Eratosthenes: cross out the multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7, and the numbers left over are the primes!

pics.alt: Portrait of Carl Friedrich Gauss in a black velvet cap
pics.caption: Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855) called number theory "the queen of mathematics".

topics.name: Trigonometry
topics.blurb: SOH CAH TOA! Use triangles to measure kites, ladders, shadows and the world.

pics.alt: A drawing of a brass navigation tool shaped like a slice of pie
pics.caption: A sextant measures the angle between the Sun or a star and the horizon. Sailors used it with trigonometry to work out where they were at sea!

pics.alt: A circle with lines for many special angles in degrees and radians
pics.caption: The unit circle with the special angles. The cosine and sine of each angle are just the x and y coordinates of its point on the circle!

topics.name: Combinatorics
topics.blurb: The art of counting without listing: outfits, line-ups, teams and grid paths!

pics.alt: A drawing of a Rubik's Cube with coloured squares
pics.caption: A Rubik's Cube can be mixed up in 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 different ways. Counting that is combinatorics!

pics.alt: Six colourful dice with 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 20 sides
pics.caption: Dice with 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 20 sides. If you roll them all at once there are 4 × 6 × 8 × 10 × 12 × 20 = 460,800 possible results. AND means multiply!

topics.name: Permutations vs Combinations
topics.blurb: Does order matter? Learn the big decision that every counting problem asks.

pics.alt: A silver padlock with a blue number dial
pics.caption: Fun fact: a "combination" lock should really be called a PERMUTATION lock, because the order of the numbers matters!

pics.alt: A hand holding an ice-cream cone with two different scoops stacked on top
pics.caption: Picking 2 flavors for a cup is a combination, but on a cone, which flavor goes on top matters. That's a permutation!

topics.name: Probability
topics.blurb: How likely is it? Complements, AND and OR rules, and expected value.

pics.alt: A tall board with pegs and small balls that have piled up at the bottom
pics.caption: A Galton board: each ball bounces left or right at random, yet together they pile up in a bell-shaped hill every time!

pics.alt: An old black-and-white drawing of a board with pegs and a funnel
pics.caption: Francis Galton's own 1889 drawing of his board, which he called a "quincunx".
